w: William the Conqueror ordered this fortress built after the Norman Conquest; it later served as the county gaol from 1220 until 1887. The keep's interior has just been reconstructed over five years to look as it did in the early 12th century, reopening in August 2025 as part of a Grade I listed museum complex.
s: A Norman keep, once the county gaol, rebuilt for 2025
_facts: Built on William the Conqueror's orders after the Norman Conquest
Used as the county gaol from 1220 to 1887
Grade I listed since 1954, including gatehouse and prison wings
Keep interior reconstructed to its early-12th-century appearance, reopened August 2025

w: Begun in 1096 under Bishop Herbert de Losinga, the cathedral's Norman core is flint and mortar faced with cream Caen limestone shipped from France. Rioters damaged it in 1272; the cloisters that followed in 1297 are the fourth-largest in England, and the 1480 spire - a stone replacement for an earlier wooden one - is still the second tallest in the country at 315 feet.
s: Caen limestone Norman cathedral with England's 2nd-tallest spire
_facts: Construction began 1096 under Bishop Herbert de Losinga
Faced in Caen limestone shipped from Normandy
Damaged by rioters in 1272, repaired by 1278
1480 spire is the second tallest in England at 315ft; cloisters (1297) are the fourth largest

w: The oldest part of this courtyard house is a 14th-century undercroft, with additions piling up over three more centuries under merchant-mayors like the Sotherton family and Joseph Paine. It takes its name from the Strangers - Protestant refugees who fled the Catholic Low Countries from 1565, some of whom lodged here. Leonard Bolingbroke turned it into a folk museum in the early 1900s and gave it to the city.
s: A 700-year merchant's house named for Protestant refugees
_facts: Oldest fabric is a 14th-century undercroft
Named after the Strangers, Protestant refugees from the Low Countries who arrived from 1565
Extended through the 17th century by mayoral families including the Sothertons
Converted into a folk museum by Leonard Bolingbroke in the early 20th century

w: Believed to be the only medieval trading hall in Northern Europe built for a single merchant, Dragon Hall rose around 1427 when the Norwich merchant Robert Toppes redeveloped the King Street site, stacking his first-floor Great Hall on top of an older 14th-century house. Archaeology beneath it has turned up traces of an Anglo-Saxon hut from around the year 1000. Since 2018 it has housed the National Centre for Writing.
s: A merchant's private trading hall, unique in Northern Europe
_facts: Built c.1427 by merchant Robert Toppes on King Street
Thought to be the only such trading hall in Northern Europe owned by one man
Archaeology beneath the site shows an Anglo-Saxon hut from c.1000
Home to the National Centre for Writing since 2018

w: Caen limestone for Norwich Cathedral came up the Yare and Wensum by barge and passed through this 15th-century watergate, via a canal the monks dug specifically for the job. The flint ferry house beside it, built in 1647, takes its name from John Pull, who ran the crossing from 1796 to 1841 - a service that continued until 1943, decades after his death.
s: The medieval watergate that floated in the cathedral's stone
_facts: 15th-century watergate used to ferry Caen stone for Norwich Cathedral
Adjoining ferry house built in 1647, Grade II* listed
Named after John Pull, who ran the ferry 1796-1841
The ferry itself operated until 1943

w: First recorded in 1155 and likely older, this church went redundant in 1542 - and then kept working anyway. The Strangers used it as a cloth exchange from 1564, then a worsted yarn market; from 1637 it served as a French church for Walloon and Huguenot refugees; later came the Swedenborgians, a Catholic Apostolic congregation, and finally a furniture warehouse until 1985.
s: A redundant church that became a cloth exchange, then a warehouse
_facts: First documented in 1155, made redundant as a parish church in 1542
Used as a cloth exchange from 1564, then a worsted yarn market
Served as a French Protestant church from 1637, later Swedenborgian and Catholic Apostolic
On the Heritage at Risk Register since 2008

w: Only Norwich's two cathedrals are bigger than this parish church, founded around 1070 by Ralph de Gael, Earl of East Anglia, and rebuilt between 1430 and 1455 into the building standing today. It occupies slightly raised ground right next to Norwich Market, and belongs to the Greater Churches Group of England's grandest parish churches.
s: Norwich's biggest parish church, next to the market
_facts: Founded c.1070 by Ralph de Gael, Earl of East Anglia
Rebuilt 1430-1455
Largest church in Norwich after the two cathedrals
Member of the Greater Churches Group

w: Locals call it St Miles. Standing where Oak Street meets Colegate, this redundant Grade I church is often reckoned the grandest in north Norwich - not for its size, but for the flint flushwork on its walls, patterned in the early 16th century and again refreshed in the 19th.
s: North Norwich's grandest church, for its flint flushwork alone
_facts: Also known as St Miles
Grade I listed, now redundant as a parish church
Located at the junction of Oak Street and Colegate
Noted for early 16th-century and 19th-century flint flushwork
